units.oneLiner: Keep every key in the slot array itself and, when the home slot is taken, probe the next slot and the next: the probes stay inside the cache line the first one fetched, Knuth's 1963 formulas say exactly what each load factor costs, and the price is clustering, which is why the table resizes before it is full and why the hash must scatter neighbors.
units.description: Linear probing on 65,536 slots against Knuth's 1963 formulas (within 1% to load 0.7) and a Python set over 1,200,000 operations: at load 0.9 a hit costs 5.315 probes but 1.540 cache lines against 2.570 and 2.570 for double hashing; clusters of 715 slots; tombstones 5.864 probes per miss against 1.698 for backward shift; a weak hash costs 1,056 probes per hit.
units.time: O(1) expected; (1 + 1/(1 - a)) / 2 probes per hit

units.plan_row: Open addressing × Linear probing. Puzzle 172, data-structures (problemSlug hash-collision-resolution, the atlas problem page carrying "Cache-friendly hashing"; sibling live lesson cuckoo-hashing-two-table-eviction-kicks). Solution open_addressing_linear_probing.py (3.0s, prints OK): linear probing with tombstone or backward-shift deletion and a rebuild at 85% live-plus-tombstones, quadratic probing (triangular offsets), double hashing (odd stride), separate chaining, Robin Hood, Fibonacci and weak hashes, a probe-and-cache-line counter (8 slots per 64-byte line, one line per chaining node). ORACLES: (1) Knuth 1963 at loads 0.25 / 0.5 / 0.7 / 0.8 / 0.9 / 0.95: hits 1.164 / 1.509 / 2.172 / 3.027 / 5.962 / 11.609 against 1.167 / 1.500 / 2.167 / 3.000 / 5.500 / 10.500, misses 1.397 / 2.510 / 5.971 / 12.655 / 50.434 / 205.639 against 1.389 / 2.500 / 6.056 / 13.000 / 50.500 / 200.500 (within 6% to 0.8, 20% beyond); (2) 1,200,000 mixed operations across six structures all matching a Python set, final sizes matching; (3) the race at load 0.9 (every key looked up, 5,000 misses): linear probing 5.315 probes/hit, 47.975/miss, 1.540 lines/hit, variance 277, max 612, longest cluster 715; Robin Hood 5.315 / 5.644 / 1.540 / 19.8 / 29; quadratic 2.850 / 12.055 / 1.951 / 16.2 / 92; double hashing 2.570 / 10.056 / 2.570 / 11.1 / 68; chaining 2.450 / 1.923 / 2.450 / 0.5 / 9; longest run by load 8 / 31 / 85 / 209 / 752 / 3,250; (4) deletion: fill to 0.7, delete half: tombstones 5.864 probes per miss (formula for 0.7: 6.056), backward shift 1.698 (formula for 0.35: 1.683); (5) weak hash (high bits) on 2,048 consecutive keys in 4,096 slots: linear probing 1,056 probes per hit, double hashing 8.3, chaining 402.8, strong hash 1.50. Honest: linear probing pays twice double hashing's probes at 0.9 and wins only on lines; the Robin Hood mean is identical to 1e-9 (the displacement total is invariant), asserted; three author notes recorded (quadratic vs double ordering; the first weak-hash experiment at 65,536 slots ran quadratic for ten minutes and was shrunk; a 5,000-key hit sample was replaced by every key after the early-inserted keys biased it). Cards: self, Hash table with chaining, Robin Hood hashing, Cuckoo hashing (live lesson badge) (all algoName). neverUse: linear probing with a hash that keeps neighbors neighbors. Figure: Knuth's hit and miss curves with the measured points beside bars of the longest run by load; cite Knuth 1963 / TAOCP 3 6.4, Amdahl et al. 1954, Pagh-Pagh-Ruzic STOC 2007 DOI 10.1145/1250790.1250839. Viz LinearProbingViz: a 64-slot table as eight cache lines filling to load 0.9, walked slots amber and touched lines outlined, the running average probes per insert against Knuth's expectation, every key checked reachable from its home each tick; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles x 21 ticks, 0 breaks; stepMs 500, holdTicks rests. Preserved narration: Aoede + Algieba.

units.oneLiner: Center a Gaussian bump of width h on every observation and average them, and set h by the one-line rule 0.9 min(s, IQR/1.34) n^(-1/5), the bandwidth that is optimal for Gaussian data with a robust scale: nearly the oracle on one cloud of points, and a blur on two, because the scale it measures is then the gap between the modes.
units.description: Kernel density estimation with Silverman's bandwidth against the exact integrated squared error of three known densities (n = 300): within 1.00x of the oracle on the Gaussian and 1.10x on the skewed density, but 5.01x on separated modes (h 0.453 against 0.227) where cross-validation reaches 1.03x; histograms 1.97x to 9.14x; the bandwidth shrinks as n^-0.167 and the error as n^-0.690.
units.time: O(n) per evaluation point; one bandwidth from s and IQR
units.baseline: Histogram with Freedman-Diaconis or Sturges bins
units.plan_row: Kernel density estimation × Silverman bandwidth. Puzzle 179, probabilistic (problemSlug density-estimation, the atlas problem page carrying "Density estimation"; sibling live lesson gaussian-mixture-expectation-maximization, puzzle 110). Solution kernel_density_estimation_silverman_bandwidth.py (1.9s, prints OK): three Marron-Wand Gaussian-mixture densities (Gaussian; skewed unimodal #2; separated bimodal #7), a Sample class with precomputed pairwise distances giving the EXACT integrated squared error of a Gaussian KDE at any bandwidth (the three Gaussian-convolution terms in closed form), Silverman's rule, Scott's rule, least-squares cross-validation (Rudemo/Bowman), the oracle bandwidth by a 30-point log grid, exact histogram ISE for Freedman-Diaconis and Sturges bins via the Gaussian CDF, and a nonnegativity and unit-mass check on a wide grid. ORACLES (n = 300): Gaussian (sd 1.03, IQR 1.43): h oracle 0.297, Silverman 0.296, Scott 0.348, LSCV 0.389; ISE multiples Silverman 1.00x, Scott 1.04x, LSCV 1.12x, histogram FD 1.97x (13 bins), Sturges 2.35x (10), h 0.03 7.3x, h 1.5 11.5x; oracle ISE 0.0047. Skewed unimodal (sd 0.83, IQR 1.01): oracle 0.260, Silverman 0.217, Scott 0.282, LSCV 0.198; 1.10x, 1.11x, 1.27x, FD 3.75x (19), Sturges 9.14x (10), 17.6x, 78.8x; oracle 0.0015. Separated bimodal (sd 1.57, IQR 2.97): oracle 0.227, Silverman 0.453, Scott 0.533, LSCV 0.198; 5.01x, 7.82x, 1.03x, FD 7.83x (7), Sturges 4.92x (10), 8.5x, 36.6x; oracle 0.0033. Rates on the Gaussian, twelve samples per n: n 50 / 100 / 200 / 400 / 800: h 0.366 / 0.340 / 0.302 / 0.264 / 0.233, ISE 0.0070 / 0.0080 / 0.0040 / 0.0026 / 0.0011; log-log slopes bandwidth -0.167 (theory -0.200), ISE -0.690 (theory -0.800). Honest: the rule loses to a ten-bin histogram on the separated modes; cross-validation loses to the rule on the Gaussian; three author corrections recorded (cross-validation expected to win everywhere; the KDE expected to beat histograms everywhere; the bandwidth slope sits above -1/5 because the robust scale is biased low at small n). Cards: self, Leave-one-out cross-validation, Gaussian mixture model (live lesson badge), Mean shift (all algoName). neverUse: the rule of thumb on data with separated modes. Figure: the bimodal truth with KDEs at h 0.227 / 0.453 / 0.03 beside the exact ISE-vs-h U with the rule, oracle, and LSCV marked; cite Silverman 1986 3.4.2, Rosenblatt 1956, Parzen 1962 DOI 10.1214/aoms/1177704472, Marron and Wand 1992. Viz KdeViz: a seeded 120-point sample from one of the three densities (by cycle), the bandwidth swept up a 30-step log ladder one step per tick, the estimate drawn against the truth, the ISE U forming on a log-log panel with Silverman's h marked; mass-to-one and ISE nonnegativity checked every tick; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles x 30 ticks, 0 breaks; opening seed 20261013 chosen by a scan (Gaussian 1.02x, skewed 1.02x, bimodal 2.72x on the first three cycles) and disclosed; stepMs 320, holdTicks rests. units.oneLiner: List every n-bit string so that neighbors differ in exactly one bit by taking the shorter list with a leading zero and then its mirror image with a leading one: the seam is one flip like every other step, the recursion collapses to g(i) = i XOR (i >> 1) with the ruler sequence naming the flipped bit, and a walk through all subsets changes one element at a time.
units.description: Gray codes by the reflected construction, equal to i XOR (i >> 1) on all 131,070 codes to 16 bits with one bit per step and a closed cycle; all 1,048,576 subset sums of 20 numbers by one operation each against 1.99998 for binary counting and 20 for recomputation; an 8-bit encoder that misreads by up to 127 positions in binary and never in Gray.
units.time: O(1) per code; O(2^n) for the walk
units.baseline: Binary counting over the power set
units.plan_row: Gray code generation × Reflected binary. Puzzle 180, dp-combinatorics (problemSlug subset-enumeration, the atlas problem page carrying "Subset enumeration"). Solution gray_code_generation_reflected_binary.py (1.4s, prints OK): the recursive mirror construction, the closed form g(i) = i XOR (i >> 1) and its prefix-XOR inverse, the trailing-zero ruler sequence, a misaligned-sensor encoder model enumerating every mixed reading of a transition, three subset-sum enumerations over 20 numbers (Gray walk with an incremental sum, binary counting with incremental updates, recomputation), binary-counting flip statistics, a lexicographic-by-size listing, and Steinhaus-Johnson-Trotter against lexicographic next-permutation. ORACLES: (1) the reflected list equals the closed form and the inverse recovers every index on all 131,070 codes for n = 1 to 16; (2) every neighbor pair at Hamming distance 1, the closing pair too, all codes distinct, the flipped bit at step i equal to trailing-zeros(i) at every step; (3) the 8-bit encoder over 256 transitions: natural binary worst misread 127 positions (mean of per-transition worst errors 3.50; the rollover 127 to 128 readable as any of 256 values), Gray worst 0 (every reading one of the two positions the shaft is between); (4) 2^20 subset sums: Gray 1,048,575 element operations (1.000 per step, 0.17 s), binary incremental 2,097,130 (1.99998 per step, 0.18 s), recompute 20,971,520 (20 per step, 0.77 s), every Gray-order sum equal to the direct sum; (5) binary counting flips per step (mean, worst) n = 4: 1.73333, 4; n = 8: 1.96863, 8; n = 12: 1.99707, 12; n = 16: 1.99976, 16, exactly (2^(n+1) - n - 2)/(2^n - 1); lexicographic listing by size at n = 12 changes 2.66 elements per step, worst 12; Steinhaus-Johnson-Trotter produces all 720 permutations of six items by adjacent swaps where lexicographic next-permutation changes 2.62 positions per step. Honest: the reflected code is unbalanced (bit zero flips half the time), unsorted, and enumerates all sizes at once, said in the weakness; two author corrections recorded (binary counting flips just under two bits per step, not log n; the encoder's worst misread is 127, half the dial, not 255). Cards: self, Powerset enumeration, Combinatorial Gray flip, Steinhaus-Johnson-Trotter (all algoName, pages present). neverUse: a natural binary absolute encoder. Figure: the reflected lists for one to four bits with mirrored halves colored, beside the per-transition worst misread of an 8-bit binary encoder (computed inline) against Gray's zero line; cite Gray US Patent 2,632,058 (1953), Gilbert BSTJ 1958 DOI 10.1002/j.1538-7305.1958.tb03887.x, Knuth TAOCP 4A 7.2.1.1. Viz GrayCodeViz: two encoder dials (3, 4, or 5 bits by cycle) advancing one position per tick, Gray beside natural binary, changed bits highlighted, possible readings and worst misread counted, the one-flip, distinctness, and closed-cycle invariants checked every tick; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 0 breaks; stepMs 700, holdTicks rests. Preserved narration: Aoede + Algieba. units.oneLiner: To move n disks, move the top n - 1 to the spare peg, move the largest disk once, and move the n - 1 back onto it: the plan is the instruction applied to itself, the count is 2^n - 1 and provably the fewest, and the same sequence falls out of an iterative rule, of binary counting, and of the Gray code.
units.description: The Tower of Hanoi recursion replayed for legality: 2^n - 1 moves for every n to 20 (1,048,575 at n = 20), proven optimal by breadth-first search to n = 8; the iterative rule, the ruler sequence, and the Gray code reproduce it; Frame-Stewart equals the four-peg optimum (33 against 255 at n = 8); a random walk needs 5,780 moves at n = 6 against 63.
units.baseline: Breadth-first search over the state graph
units.plan_row: Tower of Hanoi × Recursive halving. Puzzle 181, search-constraints-games (problemSlug tower-of-hanoi, the atlas problem page carrying "Disk-transfer puzzle"). Solution tower_of_hanoi_recursive_halving.py (0.7s, prints OK): the three-peg recursion, a legality replay on simulated pegs, legal-move enumeration and breadth-first distances over tuples of peg positions for three or four pegs, the iterative smallest-disk-cycle rule with the parity-dependent direction, the ruler and Gray-code checks, the Frame-Stewart recursion with its recurrence-chosen split over explicit disk lists, and a random legal walk with no immediate undo. ORACLES: (1) 2^n - 1 legal moves and arrival for every n from 1 to 20 (1, 3, 7, 15, 31, ..., 65,535 at 16, 1,048,575 at 20); (2) breadth-first search over 3^n states (3 to 6,561) for n = 1 to 8: optimum 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, 63, 127, 255, and the recursive state after move k at distance k; (3) the iterative rule equal to the recursion move for move for n = 1 to 12; (4) disk at step k = 1 + trailing zeros of k, and the odd-moved disks after k moves = Gray code of k, for every k below 4,096; (5) Frame-Stewart four-peg moves 1, 3, 5, 9, 13, 17, 25, 33 for n = 1 to 8, legal, equal to the recurrence and to the breadth-first four-peg optimum over 4^n states (4 to 65,536); (6) random legal walk, 20 trials each, cap 200,000: n = 3 mean 52 (10 to 191) against 7; n = 4 mean 364 (37 to 1,171) against 15; n = 5 mean 1,781 (366 to 7,940) against 31; n = 6 mean 5,780 (1,063 to 17,148) against 63. Honest: the exponential count is the floor, not the method's fault, and the three-peg recursion is far from optimal with four pegs; author correction recorded (the smallest disk's direction depends on the parity of n, not always clockwise). Cards: self, Frame-Stewart, Breadth-first search, Gray code generation (all algoName). neverUse: a random legal walk or a search that does not know the recursion. Figure: the 27-state three-disk graph as a Sierpinski triangle with the 7-move optimal path, beside log-scale moves by n for three pegs, four pegs, and the random walk; cite Lucas 1883, Frame and Stewart AMM 1941 DOI 10.2307/2304268, Bousch 2014. Viz HanoiViz: the recursion one move per tick on 4 to 7 disks with seeded source and target pegs, the moved disk amber, the binary counter, the ruler bit, and the Gray code beside the pegs, every move checked for legality and both identities checked every tick; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 0 breaks; stepMs 450, holdTicks rests. Preserved narration: Aoede + Algieba. units.oneLiner: Write the integral as the box volume times the mean of the function, estimate that mean by evaluating the function at points drawn independently and uniformly over the box, and read the error off the sample standard deviation over the square root of the count: unbiased, self-reporting, and shrinking as one over root N in any number of dimensions, where a grid of m points per axis costs m to the power d.
units.description: Monte Carlo integration by uniform sampling against exact integrals in 1, 2, 6, and 10 dimensions: the error fell as N^-0.47 to N^-0.55 in every dimension, the 95% error bar covered the truth 94.3% of the time, and in 10-D at 1,024 evaluations it erred 3% where the two-point trapezoid grid erred 58%; on an infinite-variance integrand the bar covered only 65%.
units.time: O(N) evaluations; error sigma / sqrt(N) in any dimension
units.space: a running sum and a sum of squares
units.baseline: Trapezoid rule on a product grid
units.plan_row: Monte Carlo integration × Uniform sampling. Puzzle 182, probabilistic (problemSlug numerical-integration, the atlas problem page carrying "Numerical integration"). Solution monte_carlo_integration_uniform_sampling.py (2.0s, prints OK): three integrands with closed forms (a product of smooth factors with integral exactly 1, the Gaussian over the unit cube equal to a power of (sqrt(pi)/2) erf(1), the unit ball inside its cube with volume pi^(d/2) / Gamma(d/2 + 1)), uniform-sampling Monte Carlo with the standard error, product rules for trapezoid / Simpson / five-point Gauss-Legendre weights, Halton quasi-random points on the first ten primes, stratified (one point per cell) sampling, and a log-log slope fitter. ORACLES: (1) the 1/sqrt(N) law on the product integrand, RMS error over 40 runs at N = 100 / 1,000 / 10,000: d = 1: 0.0320 / 0.0125 / 0.0036 (slope -0.474, ratio 8.9); d = 2: 0.0553 / 0.0169 / 0.0044 (-0.551, 12.7); d = 6: 0.1015 / 0.0335 / 0.0102 (-0.499, 9.9); d = 10: 0.1580 / 0.0438 / 0.0166 (-0.489, 9.5); (2) coverage of the 95% interval on the Gaussian 6-cube at N = 2,000 over 300 repetitions: 0.943, realized RMS error 0.00294 against the mean claimed standard error 0.00280; (3) rivals on the Gaussian cube at equal budgets, absolute error: d = 1 at 10,001 evaluations: Monte Carlo 1.70e-4, trapezoid 6.13e-10, Simpson 8.88e-16, Gauss-Legendre (5 points) 6.05e-9, Halton 1.08e-4, stratified 3.93e-8; d = 2 at 4,096: Monte Carlo 3.02e-3 (rms of 40), trapezoid 64 x 64 2.31e-5, Halton 2.64e-4, stratified 5.31e-5; d = 6 at 4,096: Monte Carlo 1.77e-3, trapezoid 4^6 9.32e-3, Halton 5.62e-4, stratified 4.96e-4 (exact 0.17350); d = 10 at 1,024: Monte Carlo 1.67e-3 (3% of 0.053974), trapezoid 2^10 3.16e-2 (58%), Halton 2.33e-3, stratified 8.90e-4; Simpson's coarsest 10-D grid would need 3^10 = 59,049 evaluations; the 10-ball fraction 0.00252 against 0.00249 from 200,000 points (predicted relative error 0.045, realized 0.012); (4) infinite variance, x^(-3/4) on (0, 1] with integral 4, at N = 2,000: coverage 0.650, realized RMS error 0.793 against claimed 0.465, error slope -0.420 over N = 1,000 to 100,000. Honest: Halton loses to uniform sampling in 10-D at this budget and stratified sampling beats both everywhere (author correction recorded: the draft expected Halton to win in every dimension); the hero loses by 2e11x to Simpson in 1-D and the page says so. Cards: self, Quasi-Monte Carlo, Gauss-Legendre quadrature, Stratified sampling (all algoName, all pages in dist/algo). neverUse: a product-rule grid in ten dimensions. Figure: log-log RMS error curves for four dimensions sharing the 1/sqrt(N) slope, beside per-dimension error bars for Monte Carlo, the grid, and Halton; cite Metropolis and Ulam JASA 1949 DOI 10.1080/01621459.1949.10483310, Niederreiter 1992. units.oneLiner: Keep a FIFO ready queue and let the head run for one quantum before it goes to the back: every job gets a turn within one lap of the queue, so a short job never waits out a long one, and the quantum's length is the dial between responsiveness and the cost of switching, with no knowledge of any burst required.
units.description: Round-robin with a time quantum on 60 jobs at about 76% load (switch cost 1), every schedule checked for legality and conservation: at q = 4 interactive response 11.8 against 38.0 for FCFS at utilization 0.809 against 0.947 and turnaround 82.0 against 55.1; q = 1 drops utilization to 0.523; the fairness bound held on every turn; SJF and SRTF matched exhaustive optima; a...
units.time: O(1) per dispatch; one lap of the queue per turn
units.plan_row: Round-robin scheduling × Time quantum. Puzzle 183, optimization-or (problemSlug cpu-scheduling, the atlas problem page carrying "CPU scheduling"; sibling live lessons earliest-deadline-first and rate-monotonic-shorter-period). Solution round_robin_scheduling_time_quantum.py (3.1s, prints OK): an event-driven single-CPU simulator (FCFS, SJF, SRTF with preemption on arrival, round-robin with a quantum, a three-level feedback queue 4 / 8 / 16, switch cost charged on every change of job), a legality and conservation checker, a fairness checker over every pair of consecutive turns, an exhaustive permutation referee, a dynamic program for the preemptive optimum, and a 60-job workload (interactive bursts 1 to 6, batch 20 to 80, 1,047 units of demand over 1,381 time units). ORACLES: (1) every schedule legal (no overlap, nothing before arrival, segments summing to bursts) and conserving (busy 1,047 under every policy; makespan = busy + idle + switches); (2) SJF equal to the best of 5,040 orders on 200 of 200 instances of 7 jobs released together; SRTF equal to the preemptive optimum on 100 of 100 staggered 4-job instances, strictly better than SJF on 27; (3) the fairness bound k (q + c) + c with every other job running at most once between two turns of a job, on every gap of every quantum; (4) the sweep at q = 1 / 2 / 4 / 8 / 16 / 32 / 64 / FCFS: interactive response 10.7 / 10.3 / 11.8 / 15.5 / 20.1 / 27.0 / 35.8 / 38.0, mean turnaround 233.6 / 127.8 / 82.0 / 60.6 / 55.6 / 56.8 / 57.8 / 55.1, mean waiting 216.2 / 110.3 / 64.6 / 43.2 / 38.2 / 39.4 / 40.4 / 37.7, max wait 1,171 / 703 / 428 / 247 / 179 / 150 / 171 / 147, switches 956 / 471 / 247 / 140 / 99 / 78 / 65 / 59, utilization 0.523 / 0.690 / 0.809 / 0.882 / 0.914 / 0.931 / 0.942 / 0.947; FCFS identical to q = infinity to the last digit; rivals: SJF response 17.7, turnaround 40.1, waiting 22.7, max wait 113; SRTF 1.4 / 31.7 / 14.2 / 127 (85 switches, 0.925); MLFQ 5.4 / 56.8 / 39.4 / 284 (122 switches, 0.896); (5) convoy of eight 2-unit jobs behind an 80-unit job: FCFS mean interactive response 90.5, round-robin q = 4 14.5; q = 1 with switch cost 2: utilization 0.338, turnaround 486.8 against 82.0. Honest: FCFS has the best mean turnaround and max wait here, round-robin buys response with turnaround and switches, MLFQ beats plain round-robin on both, and the 80%-of-bursts rule picks q = 36 on this bimodal mix, which responds like FCFS; three author corrections recorded (the textbook gap bound needed the closing switch and the structural every-other-job-once statement; the first workload was overloaded threefold; the quantum rule of thumb). Cards: self, Shortest processing time, Multilevel feedback queue, Completely fair scheduler (all algoName, pages present). neverUse: a quantum shorter than the context switch. Figure: response and turnaround against the quantum on a log axis with FCFS at the edge, beside utilization against the quantum; cite Corbato, Merwin-Daggett, Daley AFIPS 1962 DOI 10.1145/1460833.1460871, Kleinrock 1964 and 1976, Silberschatz chapter 5. units.oneLiner: Run m tests at once and reject each only at alpha over m: the union bound then caps the chance of any false claim across the whole family at alpha, whatever the tests' dependence, and the price is that every real effect must clear alpha over m instead of alpha.
units.description: Bonferroni against exact expectations over thousands of simulated families: uncorrected testing false-alarms 63.9% of the time at 20 nulls and 99.2% at 100, Bonferroni 4.73% and 5.07% (exact 4.88%), lower under correlation; Holm rejects a superset at the same guarantee, Benjamini-Hochberg finds 73% of real effects against 51% but lets family-wise error reach 0.32.
units.time: O(m): one threshold compared to every p-value
units.plan_row: Bonferroni correction × Family-wise error control. Puzzle 184, probabilistic (problemSlug multiple-testing, the atlas problem page carrying "Multiple testing"). Solution bonferroni_correction_family_wise_error_control.py (2.1s, prints OK): a family generator (m z-statistics, the first m1 shifted by 3.5, under independence, a common factor of correlation 0.5, or centering), exact two-sided p-values via erfc, five rules (no correction, Bonferroni alpha/m, Sidak, Holm step-down, Benjamini-Hochberg step-up), and a run that tallies family-wise error, power, and false discovery proportion while checking the set inclusions Bonferroni within Holm within BH on every family. ORACLES at alpha 0.05: (1) all-null families, FWER no correction / Bonferroni / Sidak / Holm / BH: m = 20 independent (3,000 reps) 0.639 / 0.0473 / 0.0490 / 0.0473 / 0.0473 against exact Bonferroni 0.0488 and Sidak 0.0500, se 0.0040; m = 20 common factor 0.411 / 0.0373 / 0.0380 / 0.0373 / 0.0410; m = 20 centered 0.630 / 0.0467 / 0.0480 / 0.0467 / 0.0480; m = 100 independent 0.992 / 0.0507 / 0.0513 / 0.0507 / 0.0527; m = 100 common factor 0.781 / 0.0247 / 0.0247 / 0.0247 / 0.0310; m = 100 centered 0.993 / 0.0500 / 0.0513 / 0.0500 / 0.0513; m = 1,000 (600 reps) independent 1.000 / 0.0400 / 0.0417 / 0.0400 / 0.0433, common factor 1.000 / 0.0267 / 0.0267 / 0.0267 / 0.0333, centered 1.000 / 0.0467 / 0.0467 / 0.0467 / 0.0500: Bonferroni at or below alpha in all nine; (2) nesting held on every family; (3) m = 100 with 10 effects of 3.5 se (3,000 reps): power / FWER / FDR: no correction 0.939 / 0.990 / 0.310, Bonferroni 0.511 / 0.044 / 0.008, Holm 0.516 / 0.047 / 0.008, BH 0.733 / 0.321 / 0.046 (theorem alpha m0/m = 0.045); m = 1,000 with 50 effects (600 reps): no correction 0.940 / 1.000 / 0.502, Bonferroni 0.290 / 0.038 / 0.003, Holm 0.291 / 0.038 / 0.003, BH 0.640 / 0.793 / 0.046 (theorem 0.048); (4) look-elsewhere: median smallest null p-value 0.0334 at m = 20 (theory 0.0341) and 0.0069 at m = 100 (theory 0.0069); the best of 20 subgroups clears 0.05 in 63.9% of experiments, the best of 100 in 99.2%. units.oneLiner: Turn one step of a linear recurrence into a companion matrix, so n steps are the n-th power, and take that power by squaring once per bit of n and multiplying in at the one bits: floor(log2 n) + popcount(n) - 1 products instead of n - 1, for Fibonacci at a quintillion, for walk counts on a graph, for anything associative.
units.description: Matrix exponentiation by squaring: F(20,000), 4,180 digits, from 18 matrix products equal to 20,000 iteration steps with Cassini's identity holding; F(10^18) mod 10^9 + 7 agreed by the matrix, fast doubling, and Kitamasa (209783453) in 656, 180, and 492 scalar multiplications; the product count exactly floor(log2 n) + popcount(n) - 1 on every n to 4,096; A^L equal to a walk count; recursion 1,664,079 calls for F(30).

units.oneLiner: Seal the bids, give the item to the highest, and charge the second bid: your bid then decides only whether you win, never what you pay, so the truth is a dominant strategy, the highest value always wins, and the seller earns exactly what a first-price auction would at equilibrium, without anyone computing one.
units.description: The Vickrey auction against exhaustive deviation checks and closed forms: 0 profitable deviations in 4,029,261 comparisons; the highest value wins 60,000 of 60,000 draws; revenue 0.4997 at n = 3 against first-price 0.4994 and theory 0.5; Myerson's reserve 0.5 lifts two-bidder revenue from 0.333 to 0.418; a seller shill steals 0.2496 per sale.
units.time: O(n log n) to sort the bids, O(n) with two running maxima
